newsitem.title: UK: Clarke rules out change to UK wait-and-see on EMU.
newsitem.headline: Clarke rules out change to UK wait-and-see on EMU.

text.p: British finance minister Kenneth Clarke on Monday denied as senseless and preposterous a report that the government was considering ditching its wait-and-see stance toward the European Union's planned single currency.

Clarke was reacting to a report in the Daily Telegraph newspaper that Prime Minister John Major had the backing of 18 of his 22-member cabinet for a policy shift to fight the coming general election on a pledge not to scrap the pound sterling.

"I don't believe for one moment that anything of that kind is being contemplated," he told British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC) radio. "It simply isn't going to happen. It would be senseless were it to happen."
Clarke, the leading pro-European in the cabinet, was speaking from Brussels where EU finance ministers were meeting to discuss plans for monetary union, due to start in 1999.

Major won an opt-out from the single currency when it was negotiated at the Maastricht EU summit in 1991. Since then he has stuck to the view that Britain would decide whether or not to join when the time was ripe.
This policy was reaffirmed in April by the cabinet, which also agreed that any decision to sign up for economic and monetary union (EMU) would have to be ratified by a referendum.

But since the Labour party adopted an identical stance last month, Major has come under growing pressure from "Euro-sceptics" in his deeply divided ruling Conservative party to adopt a more distinctive policy in time for the election.
Labour, the main opposition party, enjoys a lead in opinion polls of about 20 percentage points. The election must be held by May 22.

The Telegraph daily said that after months of battling with the Euro-sceptics, who oppose closer European integration on sovereignty grounds, Major had concluded that Britain should not be part of the first wave signing up for a single currency.

But Clarke, noting that the Telegraph was owned and edited "by people who hold extremely anti-European views", said he and Major had united the ruling party behind a sensible wait-and-see policy at its annual conference as recently as October.

"The idea that six weeks later we're all talking about changing it is quite preposterous in my view. It would be no way to fight an election or present yourself to the country as a governing party," Chancellor of the Exchequer Clarke said.
Clarke's firm rebuttal of a pending policy shift was the second in 24 hours from pro-Europeans in the cabinet.

Deputy Prime Minister Michael Heseltine denied a similar story in the Sunday Telegraph, the daily paper's stablemate, which said Major was ready to declare that Britan's chances of signing up for a single currency in 1999 were "very remote".

As hand-wringing in Conservative party ranks showed no signs of letting up, European Commission President Jacques Santer said Britain would come under irresistible pressure from big business and financial interests to join EMU.
He told the Financial Times no British government, whether Conservative or Labour, would be able to resist such pressure and warned the country against marginalising itself in Europe.
"Britain must be at the heart of Europe, playing a leading role," Santer said.
He said EMU would definitely go ahead as planned in 1999 and, asked to look ahead to the year 2003, added: "There will be monetary union and Britain will be a member."
